body: Is this a friendly alternative of #ifdef for gds? I think this would be cool if it allows some special defines about whether it is running in the editor or in the debugger or inthe release build.

> Is this a friendly alternative of #ifdef for gds? I think this would be cool if it allows some special defines about whether it is running in the editor or in the debugger or inthe release build.

For editor builds, you have `editor_hint` an `editor_runtime`. For template builds, you have `template`, `debug`, `release`, `template_debug`, `template_release`.

Tool scripts don't play with this yet. So, `editor` can only mean you're running the project from an editor binary, without the ability of using `editor_hint` to tell if you're actually running _within_ the editor, at the moment. However, for those cases, you can just use `editor` and make the other checks within that function, at runtime.

> At export time, the script is preprocessed to effectively strip out the functions whose target features don't fit what the target platform and export preset declare.

From looking only at the syntax, this wasn't entirely obvious to me. Not saying that's a bad thing, but if this is also the case for most other users, it might be a relevant point.

Because runtime evaluation based on feature tags and [script remapping at export time](https://godotengine.org/asset-library/asset/3451) already exist, I believe the core value of this feature is the stripping functionality.

[This comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/4234#issuecomment-1072654311) from KoBeWi describes exactly how I've used `#if` preprocessing in C# classes in Unity when using different SDK and modules.

Because of this, it would be nice to have some way to strip code inline so things don't need to be separated into function calls. In an extreme case, I could see a bit of an anti-pattern emerging where logic needs to be duplicated between a function for one feature tag and another function for a different feature tag; these functions would need to be separate because of an SDK call, but the SDK call might be only a small part of the function.

I will be honest that I haven't gone through the process of making a solution to this in Godot with GDScript, so maybe the SDK integration isn't as big of an issue as it is with C# in Unity... But after reading the comment that I linked, it sounds like the challenge in Godot is the same as C# Unity.

btw, will there be `@if_no_features()` as the opposite version of the annotation, when there are few features that should be filtered out and the corresponding code should not be compiled but you have to list the rest long string of features, which would take more time and increase the complicatability?

To me, if this solves real-world use cases, it'd be already good, even if we consider it experimental for now.

This is the primary use-case I see for this PR. Please let me know if I'm incorrect in my understanding...

Project has Android SDKs (VR packages, ad SDKs, etc.). These SDKs have GDScript addon files in the project that should not be included in other exports of the project and are thus excluded using the existing Export/Resources settings.

This PR adds the following: Any user code that interfaces with the Android SDK scripts would be within these `@if_features("android")` annotations.

When running in the editor, all scripts are included, so scripts can be parsed without error.

When exporting to PC, `android`-specific script elements are stripped. This allows the scripts to be parsed without issue.

Without this PR, this would not be as easy to do because scripts would have parsing issues due to Android SDK scripts not being included in the PC exports.

Am I understanding how this would be used?

@allenwp, you nailed it.

Elaborating, while it's true that one could still use this for features that can be checked at runtime, that'd be an antipattern. The idea is exactly what you describe: to prevent parse errors in exported projects not including certain symbols while still being able to enjoy full capabilities while at edit time (autocomplete, static typing).

Would it be feasible to have this annotation work for any given scope, including whole classes and arbitrarily indentations inside a function? 

That way you retain the simplicity of a single annotation, without needing a closing statement like #endif

It would also allow for stripping individual parts of methods, just by indenting them one level and addin the annotation.

@JoNax97, while that's technically possible, it would involve much heavier changes and put a bigger maintenance burden on all this. I chose to limit it to functions because it looked as a sweet spot where the implementation was not too complex while the flexibility was big enough.

@vnen the problem with the current style, is that is cumbersome to patch to fix or add new `has_feature` initialization, while the new one could be just matter of implementing (in the future) a new Trait.

And the "editor hint" side effect is a huge benefit for tooling, which currently needs a lot of QoL improvements.

> I feel like using the annotation makes it hard to understand the flow of the code. Looking at the example on the OP, the repetition of the functions looks cluttered and it's hard to make out which is which.

Annotations are typically used for things like pre-processing functionality, no? They're just saying "if this feature is true, include this code", which seems fairly straightfoward to me.

> I'll be honest that this idea here felt somewhat off from the beginning and I couldn't really put my finger on it. But I now see that the original proposal is just a more elegant way of solving this issue without introducing any new things into the language.

On the contrary, I think having the annotation syntax makes it very clear that the function will be processed differently, and before the rest of script processing. What we're talking about is stripping code. Having a regular function doing pre-processing work will likely lead to confusion. `preload()` for example catches a lot of people off-guard and I feel like the next version of GDScript should clearly mark this function as a special directive rather than just an ordinary function.

> Another issue I see in the test case:
> 
> ```gdscript
> @if_features("test_feature_1", "test_feature_2")
> func _various():
> 	print("other 1")
> 
> @if_features("test_feature_1", "test_feature_2")
> func _various():
> 	print("other 1 again")
> ```
> 
> The repetition of features is not an error and only one of these will be called (the first one in the text). If those are separated by many other versions, you could easily be baffled and don't understand why it's not being called. Imagine if you add another case without realizing there was already another one with the same function.

That's not my understanding of how a feature like this would work. To me this seems like it'd just be a GDScript version of the usual `#ifdef` pre-processor directive in C. When I look at this code, what I see is that if `test_feature_1` and `test_feature_2` are defined, both `_various()` definitions will be included, and a function redefinition error will occur.

Edit: Though I suppose the PR is closer to what you're describing.

> 
> OTOH, the proposal uses existing natural language concepts to achieve the same end goal. For instance, compare with this version:
> 
> ```gdscript
> func _ready():
>     if OS.has_feature("windows"):
>         _windows_implementation()
>     elif OS.has_feature("linuxbsd"):
>         if OS.has_feature("s3tc"):
>             _linux_s3tc_timplementation()
>         elif OS.has_feature("astc"):
>             _linux_astc_implementation()
> 	else:
> 		_other_implementation()
> 
> func _other_implementation():
> 	print("Other OS...")
> 
> func _windows_implementation():
> 	print("Windows!")
> 
> func _linux_s3tc_timplementation():
> 	print("Linuxxx with S3TC texture compression!")
> 
> func _linux_astc_implementation():
> 	print("Linuxxx with ASTC texture compression!")
> ```

I think I see the source of confusion here, though correct me if I'm wrong.

I don't think `@if_features` is being touted as replacing `OS.has_feature()`. You'd still be able to use that. What this PR adds is the ability to remove code that would throw errors on other platforms. Something like this:

```gdscript
func _ready():
    if OS.has_feature("android"):
        _android_setup();

@if_features("android")
func _android_setup():
    # Throws a fatal script error on Windows/Mac/Linux even when not being called
    android_sdk_function_only_defined_for_android();
```

It's less about trimming down unused code and more about allowing the script to execute without errors.

> The downside of this sample I put is naturally that all functions would be present in the export, since there's no information to remove them (we _could_ remove unused function on export but that's a whole new discussions with its own complications). One way to solve this would be concentrate the switches in a single place:
> 
> ```gdscript
> func _ready():
> 	_implementation()
> 
> func _implementation():
>     if OS.has_feature("windows"):
>         print("Windows!")
>     elif OS.has_feature("linuxbsd"):
>         if OS.has_feature("s3tc"):
>             print("Linuxxx with S3TC texture compression!")
>         elif OS.has_feature("astc"):
>             print("Linuxxx with ASTC texture compression!")
>     else:
>         print("Other OS...")
> ```

I don't think we should be stripping code at this level. It's too complicated for not much benefit (and the behind-the-scenes magic could cause confusion). Here's one example where this sort of thing falls apart:

```gdscript
var foo := false
var bar := true

func _implementation():
    if _function_with_side_effects() && OS.has_feature("windows"):
        print("Windows!")

func _function_with_side_effects():
    if !foo:
        foo = true
    return bar
```

We can't strip the `print("Windows!")` code because `_function_with_side_effects()` is in the same if statement. Otherwise we'd change the behavior of the code unexpectedly and `foo` wouldn't be set to `true`. And I can see other issues like this cropping up as well.

> We can't strip the `print("Windows!")`

We could, if we had better control flow analysis and an Intermediate Representation (since a text-based preprocessor is not easy to make, we don't have a formatter yet). After replacing the "constant expression", we get:

```gdscript
if _function_with_side_effects() && false:
  print("Windows!")
```

And while you are right that we can't discard a call with a side effect, we know for sure that the `if` body will never be executed, so the result will be:

```gdscript
_function_with_side_effects()
```

> On the contrary, I think having the annotation syntax makes it very clear that the function will be processed differently, and before the rest of script processing.

So, you can see that on the function definition side, but it's hard to see on the calling side. It's possible that you end up calling a function that won't exist. Even if does exist, you have to parse in your head which one is being called. Now, `#ifdef` has a similar problem, but that's also a reason to not have a full preprocessor.

> What we're talking about is stripping code. Having a regular function doing pre-processing work will likely lead to confusion. `preload()` for example catches a lot of people off-guard and I feel like the next version of GDScript should clearly mark this function as a special directive rather than just an ordinary function.

The regular function won't be doing pre-processing. We'll only add means for it to be evaluated at compile time, including the variations on export. The `if` is the one becoming special, which a GDScript keyword, not a function.

Is not even near what `preload()` does. Which is not really a "function", it just looks like one. And I'm not even defending  `preload()` itself, it will eventually be deprecated and removed.

> That's not my understanding of how a feature like this would work. To me this seems like it'd just be a GDScript version of the usual `#ifdef` pre-processor directive in C. When I look at this code, what I see is that if `test_feature_1` and `test_feature_2` are defined, both `_various()` definitions will be included, and a function redefinition error will occur.
> 
> Edit: Though I suppose the PR is closer to what you're describing.

What I'm describing is exactly how this PR works. I literally took the example from the test cases here. It's already tripping you up, because it's not clear how it works.

> I don't think `@if_features` is being touted as replacing `OS.has_feature()`. You'd still be able to use that. What this PR adds is the ability to remove code that would throw errors on other platforms. Something like this:
> 
> ```gdscript
> func _ready():
>     if OS.has_feature("android"):
>         _android_setup();
> 
> @if_features("android")
> func _android_setup():
>     # Throws a fatal script error on Windows/Mac/Linux even when not being called
>     android_sdk_function_only_defined_for_android();
> ```
> 
> It's less about trimming down unused code and more about allowing the script to execute without errors.

What I'm saying is that `if OS.has_feature("android")` is enough, we don't need the annotation. This sample would actually give an error exactly because the `_android_setup()` function is not defined in the PC editor but in `_ready()` you are calling it and the analysis still run inside the `if` block. No one is thinking we would remove `has_feature()` function.

Both trimming and avoiding errors can be done with `if` itself.

> I don't think we should be stripping code at this level. It's too complicated for not much benefit (and the behind-the-scenes magic could cause confusion). Here's one example where this sort of thing falls apart:
> 
> ```gdscript
> var foo := false
> var bar := true
> 
> func _implementation():
>     if _function_with_side_effects() && OS.has_feature("windows"):
>         print("Windows!")
> 
> func _function_with_side_effects():
>     if !foo:
>         foo = true
>     return bar
> ```
> 
> We can't strip the `print("Windows!")` code because `_function_with_side_effects()` is in the same if statement. Otherwise we'd change the behavior of the code unexpectedly and `foo` wouldn't be set to `true`. And I can see other issues like this cropping up as well.

As @dalexeev said, we could replace the block with `_function_with_side_effects()` and it would be equivalent.

But we don't need to go that far. If you are putting other things in the condition that cannot be evaluated at compile time, the condition simply won't be evaluated at compile time. There will be no trimming nor skipping analysis in this case. It will be treated as any other dynamic conditional block. And I think most people can see that this cannot be evaluated at compile time and would not expect it to be.

> What I'm saying is that `if OS.has_feature("android")` is enough, we don't need the annotation. This sample would actually give an error exactly because the `_android_setup()` function is not defined in the PC editor but in `_ready()` you are calling it and the analysis still run inside the `if` block. No one is thinking we would remove `has_feature()` function.
> 
> Both trimming and avoiding errors can be done with `if` itself.

But what about `android_sdk_function_only_defined_for_android()`? How do we avoid analyzing that? That's going to throw an error if we don't strip it during preprocessing. This is specifically the use case I am looking for in code stripping, as allenwp mentioned [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/102083#issuecomment-2619663697).

> But what about `android_sdk_function_only_defined_for_android()`? How do we avoid analyzing that? That's going to throw an error if we don't strip it during preprocessing. This is specifically the use case I am looking for in code stripping, as allenwp mentioned [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/102083#issuecomment-2619663697).

We strip during processing. The analyzer will skip the contents of the `if` block when the condition is determined to be `false` at compile time. We don't need to do it beforehand.

> It doesn't matter whether that logic is inside `OS.has_feature()` or `if` parsing logic, it's still a special case that could trip users up.

I'm saying that the annotation proposed here would also trip people up (already tripped you before). The way it is done here is confusing. But also, anything we add can be misused or misunderstood.

> This can especially be an issue with multi-person projects where more than one person is contributing to the code. If one person doesn't know what `OS.has_feature()` is doing behind the scenes (especially because it looks like a regular function), they might add the `is_initialized` check to the same `if` statement and cause the stripping to break. Then another maintainer, who isn't working on Android, suddenly wonders why the code broke for them. They look and see that `OS.has_feature("android")` is still there. The documentation says it will strip the code. But they're unaware of this corner case. If the function were marked specially, a lot of this hassle can probably be avoided.

IMO the docs should be clearer about this, so if they read the documentation they would understand the problem. Also, in this case it would show the error in the editor because it would be now evaluating the block, so it's not like it would be invisible.

If we're talking hypothetical scenarios, the annotation could also fail. Imagine something like this:

```gdscript

func _ready():
	_implementation()

# [...] lots of other functions including _implementation for some platforms.

@if_features("android")
func _implementation():
	# Do Android-specific stuff.
	pass
```

Now another contributor wants to do an implementation for Android without realizing there's already one done in the midst of the many functions, so they add a new one at the beginning:

```gdscript

func _ready():
	_implementation()

@if_features("android")
func _implementation():
	# New function for Android.
	pass

# [...] lots of other functions including _implementation for some platforms.

@if_features("android")
func _implementation():
	# Do Android-specific stuff.
	pass
```

Now only the first one will be called and there will be no error about the repeated function. This contributor will be satisfied but it'll take a while for other people realize that now there's some code not running anymore. It doesn't matter if they read the documentation, they need to realize that there's a duplicate function.

The opposite could also happen: they add a function at the end and don't understand why it isn't being called.

----

If we really want to be more explicit, we can add a `constexpr` keyword like in C++:

```gdscript
constexpr if OS.has_feature("android"):
	pass
```

This way if the condition can't be analyzed at compile time, it would throw a compiler error. Although even if we add this I wouldn't make it mandatory.

I still prefer to use what we already have in the language. Anything we come up with will always have drawbacks and potential for misunderstanding.

> We strip during processing. The analyzer will skip the contents of the if block when the condition is determined to be false at compile time. We don't need to do it beforehand.

However if you use a class like `EditorPlugin` which gets stripped out by godot itself in a release build (because it doesn't have the "editor" feature) the parser itself will fail before having the chance to reach runtime

if you change OS.has_feature() for a builtin method that can be processed as a constant, then the processor could parse the condition as a constant and optimize out the content, but there's no warrantee that is going to happen, would depend on how the code is written.

consider the case
```
    if some_condition() && OS.has_feature("windows"):
        _some_variant = EditorClass.new()
```
even if the compiler replaces `OS.has_feature("windows")` for the constant `false` that doesn't mean you can strip out the next line, because you would have an if condition without a block, it needs to at least be repalced by `pass`

> Now another contributor wants to do an implementation for Android without realizing there's already one done in the midst of the many functions, so they add a new one at the beginning

User is not meant to do that, that's a bug, if this PR is allowing to do that, it needs to be fixed and and error complaining about redefinition of variable or function should be prompted at export time.
I havent check the code, but maybe at parse time, the gdscript analyzer could cleck the list of export targets and run a list of test for each set of features for every platform, so it can catch this kind of thing without having to wait until you try to export the game

> However if you use a class like `EditorPlugin` which gets stripped out by godot itself in a release build (because it doesn't have the "editor" feature) the parser itself will fail before having the chance to reach runtime

It is all the same, if the class isn't available but the code is being skipped during analysis, it won't give any error.

> if you change OS.has_feature() for a builtin method that can be processed as a constant, then the processor could parse the condition as a constant and optimize out the content, but there's no warrantee that is going to happen, would depend on how the code is written.
> 
> consider the case
> 
> ```
>     if some_condition() && OS.has_feature("windows"):
>         _some_variant = EditorClass.new()
> ```
> 
> even if the compiler replaces `OS.has_feature("windows")` for the constant `false` that doesn't mean you can strip out the next line, because you would have an if condition without a block, it needs to at least be repalced by `pass`

Already mentioned this before, if the condition cannot be fully evaluated at compile time it won't be. We won't be stripping only part of a condition, it's all or nothing (we _can_ replace the call to just `false` or `true` in the generated bytecode to improve performance a bit, but it won't be replaced in the source code text).

The same way a user need to know about `@if_features` to use it, they would need to know about what can be stripped or not (and honestly it's very simple). The difference is that even unaware users might be benefiting if it's something integrated with the language.

> User is not meant to do that, that's a bug, if this PR is allowing to do that, it needs to be fixed and and error complaining about redefinition of variable or function should be prompted at export time.
> I havent check the code, but maybe at parse time, the gdscript analyzer could cleck the list of export targets and run a list of test for each set of features for every platform, so it can catch this kind of thing without having to wait until you try to export the game

I agree with this. However, I'm not sure if how far we'd get with that is worth it. I mean, we could detect if two occurences of a given function have _the same exact_ set of features and warn about it. Nonetheless, since overlapping sets of features are fine because this is designed so you can have multiple matches with only the first one prevailing, that's the most we can do about this.

---

Regarding other points discussed:
- Users not understanding which functions got stripped down or why a function wasn't called.
  This is not exactly a showstopper. Further information can be given to users in addition to what the exporter already tells. However, let's bear in mind that is is not intended to be used much in a single project, but only in a few key places.
- The syntax feeling unnatural.
  It's just an annotation. And I believe it makes sense that, given it does something regular parsing-compiling of GDScript doesn't (stripping), it's a good thing that it stands out. Having builtin stripping of unused script might be a good thing, but it would then make things hard for users that need some pieces of scripting to be stripped with 100% certainty. They would then need to understand, and keep up-to-date, with the stripping rules.

> Already mentioned this before, if the condition cannot be fully evaluated at compile time it won't be. We won't be stripping only part of a condition, it's all or nothing (we can replace the call to just false or true in the generated bytecode to improve performance a bit, but it won't be replaced in the source code text).

That is not how code evaluation works, an if condition evaluates from left to right, if `some_condition()` makes some change to some variable as @KeyboardDanni mentioned, user will expect it to be excecuted. You cannot stript the entire if condition/block

The main issue I can see with this is we'd have to make sure that the matching is exhaustive. I.e. we should never allow a case where it fails to generate a function. We could address that by requiring the use of `@else` (which would throw a script error if missing). It'd be like enforcing the use of `_:` in a `match` statement.

Having said that, as long as we have error checking logic to ensure that `_implementation()` isn't redefined outside this particular `@if_features` block, I see it as a big improvement over the current proposed logic.

well, if you provide an implementation for every set of features, you should not need a default implementation, in such case parser would throw an `undefined _implementation() method` error for the platform you want to export

The problem is I don't think we have a concept of an "exhaustive set of features" besides whether a feature is available or unavailable. That is why I initially proposed that `@if_features` allows only the definition of a featureful function and a fallback function. Because that's the only way you're guaranteed to have an exhaustive match and thus always have the function defined. If we add `@elif_features`, I think we should make `@else` a requirement to avoid leaving the function undefined.

Unless I'm overestimating the importance of keeping the function defined. Maybe we *should* just let the script error if the code runs on an unexpected set of feature flags.

> Would stripping support early returns?

This requires better control flow graph analysis that takes constant expressions into account to remove dead/unreachable code. Maybe we should introduce CFG and optimize/compile it instead of AST directly.

But the problem here is not the runtime, it's that the parser/analyzer/compiler runs not only in the editor but also in the exported project, which doesn't have editor classes, causing analyzer errors. If we had an Intermediate Representation, we could avoid the parse/analyze/compile step in the exported project and load the compiled bytecode directly. This way we wouldn't have to worry about stripping code or binary tokens when exporting the project.

It seems to me that there are a number of features that we should postpone until we do the next massive refactoring and cleanup of the GDScript implementation. Because then they would be much easier to implement than they are now.

Let's not lose the perspective that the point of this PR is having a simple implementation that does the trick. That's why everything revolves around the single `@if_features` annotation, without any extra annotations or keywords. It doesn't require any sort of tree shaking nor catches users into wondering about the results of complicated rules. It is first-match-wins, with the only exception being the default one.

All this is notwithstanding that in the future something more surgical can be introduced, maybe deprecating this feature, which can also be marked experimental to see how users deal with it.

Thanks for taking time to discuss this. It looks to me that there's some misunderstanding on how this feature works and how it's intended to be used.

The fact that at edit time all of the functions are parsed in search of syntax errors is deliberate and a huge improvement over what a plain preprocessor would be able to achieve. With a preprocessor, you'd only have your feature-dependent GDScript parsed on exported projects already running on the target. I can't see why you'd ever want otherwise.

Moreover, at export time, stripping happens more similarly to how a preprocessor would do it. The non-matching functions don't make it to the export at all.

So I was also in the meeting where we were discussing this PR. I'm not sure if this implementation is the way to go now. It's too verbose, and the order in which the function overloads are processed is unclear. I've come around to the idea of using `OS.has_feature()` and using `constexpr` to guarantee that the code is stripped (if the expression fails to resolve it throws an error so you can tell that something went wrong). While an `#ifdef` style preprocessor directive would make this easy to implement, it can lead to messy code and therefore mistakes. And I don't know if doing it via function annotations is a great idea either (usually you want one function and not the other, so there needs to be some awareness of both candidates together, whereas an annotation generally considers functions in isolation).

> It doesn't require any sort of tree shaking nor catches users into wondering about the results of complicated rules. It is first-match-wins, with the only exception being the default one.

I don't think there should be any exception here. I can't see a use case for it. If you want a default, it should be the one at the bottom. Having the default be first is confusing because it looks like it'll be the candidate that's chosen every time, when it isn't.

> All this is notwithstanding that in the future something more surgical can be introduced, maybe deprecating this feature, which can also be marked experimental to see how users deal with it.

I don't think we should introduce a feature if we immediately plan to deprecate it later. Not unless we're already about to break compatibility (e.g. the jump from 3.x to 4.x) and need a stopgap right now.

I've realized, and it's my fault not having done earlier, that those with power or influence to decide don't feel good about this approach, beyond any specific points discussed. So, at this point, where we have a situation of incompatibility of tastes, it doesn't quite make sense to keep spending time here.

For what it's worth, I think with a few adjustments this idea could be considered "good enough". I'm not sure how others feel about it though. Main thing for me would be changing the candidate selection logic so it always picks the first matching candidate. Or just don't have any candidate selection logic at all and just go the `#ifdef` style route, though it has its pitfalls. But it was apparently [good enough for Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html).

But yeah, it seems like much of the team is drifting away from this as a solution. Doing it through branch elimination still feels a bit weird to me, but as long as there's a way to guarantee the code is actually removed, I could see it as being easier for end users to write.

Coming back to this (sorry for taking this long), the problem is not only that. Having the function parsed itself is okay, but you can't really type-check it because it maybe relying on things that are platform-exclusive (e.g. a mobile plugin not available on the editor platform). This would be a main use case for this kind of feature, so we can't just let users work around it. Therefore it does not provide full benefit of parsing besides syntax analysis.

The other issue is the picking heuristic. It's not obvious at all and already has been misinterpreted in this thread alone (which is majorly followed by experienced programmers). For me there are multiple ways that picking could be done, and that alone is an issue because the user would have similar ideas without knowing which one was the implemented one.

A full standard pre-processor, while not having the benefit of syntax analysis (it still could have though, if we really wanted), it's much more predictable. I do believe we might not even need that with constant `if` expressions, but if that turns out not enough, including a pre-processor would still be possible. We could even have a proper macro system if done right.

The intention in this PR is good and we want a way of doing this. In fact, at first thought, using annotations for this does sound obvious and elegant. But when we get to the nitty-gritty details, it's very difficult to make it work in a straight-forward way. In the end the design proposed is confusing for users and that's ultimately what made us reject the concept.
